event: The United States Energy Information Administration reported that Middle Eastern oil producers reduced output by more than 11 million barrels per day following a closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

verified_facts.statement: The United States Energy Information Administration reported a reduction in Middle Eastern oil output of more than 11 million barrels per day
verified_facts.note: Primary source claim; EIA is the authoritative U.S. energy statistics agency

verified_facts.statement: The Strait of Hormuz experienced a closure event
verified_facts.note: Confirmed across all framings; specific dates and causation disputed

verified_facts.statement: The Strait of Hormuz is a critical maritime chokepoint for global oil transit
verified_facts.note: Standard reference: ~20-21 mb/d historically transited through Hormuz pre-disruption

verified_facts.statement: Oil prices rose significantly during the disruption period
verified_facts.note: All framings acknowledge price increases; specific price levels ($117–138/b Brent) cited but require verification against commodity price records

verified_facts.statement: The United States is the world's largest oil producer
verified_facts.note: Confirmed by EIA data; U.S. surpassed Saudi Arabia and Russia circa 2018

verified_facts.statement: U.S. oil imports from the Persian Gulf are less than 3% of total U.S. oil consumption
verified_facts.note: Verifiable from EIA import data; reflects post-2015 U.S. crude export ban lift and shale production

unverified_shared_claims.statement: A U.S.-Israeli military strike on Iran occurred on February 28, 2026
unverified_shared_claims.note: Date is in the future relative to typical knowledge cutoffs; requires confirmation of actual event occurrence and date

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Joint Chiefs of Staff issued warnings before February 2026 strikes that Hormuz closure would result
unverified_shared_claims.note: Specific internal military communication; would require declassified or leaked official record

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Iran deliberately closed the Strait of Hormuz as a counter-measure to U.S.-Israeli strikes
unverified_shared_claims.note: Causal attribution and intent; Iran's official statements and actions are documented, but deliberate causation is interpretive

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Pipeline bypass capacity is limited to 2.6–5.5 mb/d versus 20 mb/d historical Hormuz flows
unverified_shared_claims.note: Technical infrastructure claim; requires verification against pipeline capacity databases (Suez, Sumed, Saudi-Yanbu, UAE pipelines)

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Spain's electricity prices remained low (~57% renewables) while Singapore's prices spiked to $200/MWh (95% gas-dependent)
unverified_shared_claims.note: Specific price and generation-mix data; requires verification against grid operator records (REE, EMA) during disruption period

unverified_shared_claims.statement: 30% of global urea trade transits the Strait of Hormuz
unverified_shared_claims.note: Fertilizer trade statistic; requires verification against trade flow databases (UN Comtrade, ITC)

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Gulf states are 80%+ dependent on caloric food imports
unverified_shared_claims.note: Food security statistic; verifiable from FAO/World Bank data but requires confirmation of current figure

unverified_shared_claims.statement: IRGC is charging transit fees for passage through the Strait
unverified_shared_claims.note: Reported allegation; requires confirmation from shipping industry reports, insurance records, or official Iranian statements

unverified_shared_claims.statement: Desalination plants in Kuwait and Qatar were attacked
unverified_shared_claims.note: Specific military/infrastructure incident; requires confirmation from official statements or credible reporting

points_of_disagreement: Whether the 11 mb/d reduction is the 'largest supply disruption in history' or comparable to 1970s crises (Historic Supply Shock vs. other framings' contextualization)
Whether the closure was a deliberate Iranian counter-measure to U.S.-Israeli strikes or an independent Iranian action (War Accountability vs. Geopolitical Power Realignment)
Whether the U.S.-Israeli strikes were justified or foreseeable/preventable (War Accountability vs. U.S. Energy Independence framing's focus on domestic insulation)
Whether the Hormuz closure is primarily a vulnerability of fossil fuel infrastructure (Clean Energy Transition) or a geopolitical chokepoint problem (Energy Security Vulnerability)
Whether Iran's closure and potential transit-fee system are legal under UNCLOS freedom of transit passage (International Law framing vs. others accepting closure as fait accompli)
Whether the U.S. counter-blockade is a legitimate response or itself a violation of international maritime law (International Law framing)
Whether the primary harm is to global markets/recession risk (Historic Supply Shock) or to vulnerable developing nations and Gulf civilians (Global South framing)
Whether U.S. domestic oil production insulates American consumers from price spikes (U.S. Energy Independence framing's critique) or whether global oil pricing makes this irrelevant
Whether the disruption strengthens or weakens Russia's geopolitical position (Geopolitical Power Realignment vs. implicit disagreement in other framings)
shared_foundation.summary: All framings accept that Middle Eastern oil output fell by 11+ mb/d following a Strait of Hormuz closure, that oil prices rose significantly, and that the Strait is a critical global chokepoint. They diverge sharply on causation (deliberate Iranian counter-measure vs. independent action), legality (UNCLOS compliance), historical magnitude, primary beneficiaries/losers, and whether the crisis vindicates fossil fuel vulnerability or geopolitical dependence arguments.

framings.name: Historic Supply Shock / Market Disruption
framings.question: How severe is this disruption to global oil markets, and what are the macroeconomic consequences?
framings.key_claim: The Hormuz closure and associated production shut-ins constitute the largest oil supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, triggering recession-level price and inflation pressures worldwide.
framings.description: This framing treats the EIA production data as evidence of an unprecedented market event, benchmarking it against prior shocks (1973, 1979, 1990). It centers price trajectories, inventory drawdowns, and downstream economic damage—inflation, GDP contraction, stagflation risk—as the primary story.
framings.emphasizes: Scale of output lost (10–11+ mb/d shut-in), Brent price surge past $117–138/b, global inventory depletion at record pace, recession probability, comparison to 1970s oil crises
framings.downplays: Causes of the military conflict, human casualties, geopolitical power shifts, long-term structural alternatives

The Oil Supply Shock Will Scar the World for Years (OilPrice.com, April 2026)

carriers.name: International Energy Agency (IEA)
carriers.excerpt: "the greatest threat to global energy security in history"
carriers.role_evidence: IEA's March 2026 Oil Market Report was the earliest major institutional publication quantifying the 10+ mb/d disruption and coining the 'largest supply disruption' benchmark language that all subsequent coverage cites.

carriers.name: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA)
carriers.excerpt: "production shut-ins averaged 10.5 million barrels per day in April"
carriers.role_evidence: EIA's April 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook and associated press release provided the specific shut-in figures (10.5–10.8 mb/d) that anchored global coverage of the supply shock.

carriers.name: World Bank
carriers.excerpt: "the largest oil supply shock on record, with an initial reduction in global oil supply of about 10 million barrels per day"
carriers.role_evidence: World Bank Commodity Markets Outlook April 2026 amplified the supply-shock framing to global development and finance audiences, projecting inflation and GDP impacts in developing economies.

carriers.name: OilPrice.com
carriers.excerpt: "forcing more than 10 million barrels per day of crude output shut-ins across the Middle Eastern oil producers"
carriers.role_evidence: Energy-specialist outlet synthesizing IEA/EIA data for a mass audience of traders and industry readers; widely cited in financial media.

carriers.name: Dallas Fed / Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas
carriers.excerpt: "a shortfall close to 20 percent, making this geopolitical event three to five times larger"
carriers.role_evidence: Published a quantitative historical comparison framing the Hormuz shock as 3–5x the magnitude of 1973/1979 shocks, giving the 'historic' framing academic credibility early in the crisis.

carriers.name: Kpler
carriers.excerpt: "supply is being disrupted in real time"
carriers.role_evidence: Commodities intelligence firm provided real-time tanker-tracking data confirming the supply-shock framing on Day 1 of the crisis, widely used by financial analysts.

carriers.name: Brookings Institution
carriers.excerpt: "the largest disruption in the history of the oil market"
carriers.role_evidence: Part of Brookings' 'Blowback' series; uses supply-shock framing as a baseline while shifting emphasis toward policy implications.

framings.name: Energy Security Vulnerability / Chokepoint Dependence
framings.question: Does this crisis expose structural weaknesses in global energy supply chains and the strategic risk of chokepoint dependence?
framings.key_claim: The Hormuz closure reveals that the global energy system was dangerously over-reliant on a single maritime chokepoint, with no adequate alternative infrastructure to absorb a full disruption.
framings.description: This framing interrogates the system design that allowed ~20% of global oil supply to flow through a single 21-mile-wide strait. It foregrounds inadequate bypass capacity, insufficient strategic reserves, and the failure of decades of energy security planning.
framings.emphasizes: Limited pipeline bypass capacity (~2.6–5.5 mb/d vs 20 mb/d flows), SPR levels, IEA emergency releases, absence of alternative LNG routes for Qatar, policy failures preceding the crisis
framings.downplays: Immediate price movements, the identity of the belligerents, renewable energy alternatives
sample_headlines: Hormuz closure and related production outages are key drivers in EIA's latest forecast (EIA Press Release, April 7, 2026)
Strait of Hormuz disruptions: Implications for global trade and development (UNCTAD, March 2026)
From chokepoint to crisis: The Strait of Hormuz and global oil markets (Brookings, June 2026)

carriers.name: IEA — Strait of Hormuz Emergency Response page
carriers.excerpt: "any disruption to flows through the Strait would have huge consequences for world oil markets"
carriers.role_evidence: IEA's dedicated chokepoint emergency page, continuously updated since 2025, established the authoritative data infrastructure (bypass capacity estimates, LNG exposure) that grounds this framing.

carriers.name: Congressional Research Service (CRS)
carriers.excerpt: "Congressional concern has risen in the wake of the February-March 2026 conflict as regional stability remains uncertain"
carriers.role_evidence: CRS report R45281 formalized the chokepoint-vulnerability framing for Congress, citing the need for oversight on military options and sanctions to protect energy security.

carriers.name: UNCTAD
carriers.excerpt: "The resulting ripple effects go far beyond the region, affecting energy markets, maritime transport and global supply chains"
carriers.role_evidence: UN Trade and Development published a formal report adopting the chokepoint-dependence framing, extending it to developing-world trade and food-system vulnerabilities.

carriers.name: Institute for Energy Research (IER)
carriers.excerpt: "The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed by Iran since the beginning of the conflict, choking off a vital route"
carriers.role_evidence: Conservative-leaning energy policy think tank amplified the vulnerability framing while adding a pointed critique of depleted U.S. strategic petroleum reserves.

carriers.name: Speed Commerce / Supply Chain Analysis
carriers.excerpt: "the world's most important shipping strait is blocked"
carriers.role_evidence: Widely shared data explainer synthesizing IEA and EIA bypass-capacity figures for a logistics and supply-chain audience.

carriers.name: House of Commons Library
carriers.excerpt: "almost no shipping has used the strait and it remains effectively closed"
carriers.role_evidence: UK Parliament's research arm produced a briefing on reopening the Strait, institutionally adopting the vulnerability framing and linking it to diplomatic and military response options.

framings.name: Geopolitical Power Realignment
framings.question: Who wins and who loses strategic power as a result of the disruption, and how does it redraw global influence?
framings.key_claim: The Hormuz closure is redistributing geopolitical power—benefiting Russia, U.S. shale, and Iran's leverage—while stranding Gulf producers and forcing Asian importers into emergency supply diplomacy.
framings.description: This framing focuses on the geopolitical winners and losers produced by the disruption: Russia's windfall from redirected demand, U.S. shale's opportunity, Iran's coercive leverage, China and India's scramble for alternatives, and the collapse of the Gulf Cooperation Council's economic model.
framings.emphasizes: Russia's competitive gain, U.S. blockade, China/India supply diplomacy, Iran's chokepoint leverage, collapse of GCC economic model, IRGC transit-fee extortion reports
framings.downplays: Humanitarian costs, domestic consumer pain, climate implications
sample_headlines: The Strait of Hormuz Closure and the Reshaping of Energy Geopolitics (Gulf International Forum, June 2026)
The Hormuz Crisis and China's Energy Security Dilemma (The Diplomat, May 2026)
US-Iran: Strait of Hormuz crisis reshapes global oil markets (Kpler, March 2026)

carriers.name: Gulf International Forum
carriers.excerpt: "The biggest geopolitical beneficiary is Moscow"
carriers.role_evidence: One of the first sustained analytical pieces naming specific geopolitical winners and losers—Russia, U.S. shale, Iran—from the disruption, framing it as a permanent realignment rather than a temporary shock.

carriers.name: The Diplomat
carriers.excerpt: "the Hormuz crisis reveals the limits of this model"
carriers.role_evidence: Asia-Pacific foreign policy publication that developed the China-specific power-realignment sub-framing, focusing on Beijing's dual chokepoint dilemma and overland corridor limitations.

carriers.name: Kpler
carriers.excerpt: "The conflict is materially improving Russia's competitive position in crude oil markets"
carriers.role_evidence: Commodity intelligence firm was among the first to quantify Russia's market advantage and India/China's pivot to Russian crude, giving the power-realignment framing data-grounded credibility.

carriers.name: World Economic Forum
carriers.excerpt: "The US imports relatively little oil through Hormuz, so its Asian peers bear an overwhelming share of the burden"
carriers.role_evidence: WEF amplified the asymmetric-burden sub-framing to a global elite audience, highlighting that the U.S. imposed a military action whose economic costs fall disproportionately on Asia.

carriers.name: Brookings Institution
carriers.excerpt: "Allowing Iran to charge a toll in the Strait of Hormuz is deeply problematic"
carriers.role_evidence: Brookings 'Blowback' series piece flagged IRGC transit-fee extortion as a new form of geopolitical leverage, amplifying the power-realignment framing to a policy and media audience.

carriers.name: Wikipedia — 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis
carriers.excerpt: "The crisis contributed to increased European imports of Russian liquefied natural gas"
carriers.role_evidence: Continuously updated Wikipedia article aggregating geopolitical winner/loser facts (Russia LNG gains, India/Pakistan supply diplomacy, China/Russia UN veto) for the broadest possible audience.

framings.name: Clean Energy Transition Catalyst
framings.question: Does this crisis prove that fossil fuel dependence is the true energy security risk, and should it accelerate the shift to renewables?
framings.key_claim: The Hormuz disruption exposes fossil fuel supply chains—not renewable energy intermittency—as the primary energy security vulnerability, and constitutes a once-in-a-generation argument for accelerating the clean energy transition.
framings.description: This framing recasts the crisis as vindication of the energy transition argument: that traded fossil fuels routed through choke points are inherently fragile, while domestically generated renewables are not. It calls on governments to resist locking in new fossil fuel infrastructure and instead accelerate electrification, solar, wind, and green fuels.
framings.emphasizes: Fossil fuel vulnerability vs. renewable resilience, contrast between Spain's low post-Hormuz electricity prices (57% renewables) and Singapore's $200/MWh prices (95% gas), IEA/UNFCCC calls for transition acceleration
framings.downplays: Short-term constraints on transition (grid, financing, China supply-chain dependence), coal and LNG expansion as near-term substitutes, transition costs during crisis
sample_headlines: Hormuz crisis shows clean energy is key to reducing the economic cost of fossil fuel dependence (Energy Transitions Commission, May 2026)
How the Strait of Hormuz standoff flipped the energy security debate (CNBC, June 2026)
Hormuz and the Energy Transition: Change Doesn't Just Happen (CFR, June 2026)

carriers.name: Energy Transitions Commission (ETC)
carriers.excerpt: "fossil fuel dependence is not only a climate risk but also an economic and strategic vulnerability"
carriers.role_evidence: ETC published 'Lessons on Energy Security after the Hormuz Crisis' as the definitive originating document for the transition-catalyst framing, with specific policy prescriptions and a 2035 displacement roadmap.

carriers.name: CNBC
carriers.excerpt: "fossil fuels are now intermittent and uncertain, which, of course, was the argument levelled against renewables"
carriers.role_evidence: CNBC's coverage from the Eurelectric Power Summit brought the transition-catalyst framing to a mainstream global business audience, amplifying statements from Fortum, Statkraft, and Ember CEOs/strategists.

carriers.name: IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol (via The Guardian)
carriers.excerpt: "Governments will review their energy strategies. There will be a significant boost to renewables and nuclear power"
carriers.role_evidence: IEA Executive Director's public statements gave the transition-catalyst framing authoritative institutional backing, quoted in CFR and Guardian.

carriers.name: UNFCCC Executive Secretary Simon Stiell
carriers.excerpt: "Renewables offer safer, cheaper, cleaner energy that can't be held captive by narrow shipping straits"
carriers.role_evidence: UNFCCC head adopted the transition-catalyst framing at a climate preparatory meeting, linking Hormuz directly to the 2026 UN climate summit agenda.

carriers.name: Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) — Climate Realism Initiative
carriers.excerpt: "there is nothing intrinsic about this crisis that guarantees those alternatives will be carbon-free"
carriers.role_evidence: CFR's Climate Realism Initiative pushes back on the automatic transition-catalyst assumption, noting coal expansion, grid constraints, and 1970s historical parallels where transition did not follow shock.

carriers.name: World Economic Forum
carriers.excerpt: "Geopolitical disruption to fossil fuel supply is both a strong long-term argument for accelerating renewables deployment and a powerful short-term brake"
carriers.role_evidence: WEF amplified the transition framing while adding nuance about short-term fossil fuel subsidies acting as a brake—reaching a global policymaker audience.

carriers.name: Ember (Kingsmill Bond, energy strategist)
carriers.excerpt: "fossil fuels are now intermittent and uncertain"
carriers.role_evidence: Ember's energy strategist coined the key rhetorical inversion—'fossil fuels are now the intermittent ones'—that became the framing's defining soundbite, quoted in CNBC.

framings.name: U.S. Energy Independence / Domestic Production Vindication
framings.question: Does the crisis validate or challenge claims of U.S. energy independence, and what does it mean for America's domestic energy posture?
framings.key_claim: Despite the U.S. being the world's largest oil producer and importing less than 3% of its oil from the Persian Gulf, American consumers are still suffering price spikes—exposing 'energy independence' as a political slogan rather than economic insulation.
framings.description: This framing interrogates the political narrative of U.S. energy independence against the reality that oil is a globally fungible commodity. It is contested from two directions: by those who argue the crisis proves the U.S. should expand domestic fossil fuel production further, and by those who argue it proves the meaninglessness of fossil-fuel-based 'independence.'
framings.emphasizes: U.S. record domestic production, sub-3% Persian Gulf import share, but continuing domestic gasoline/diesel price spikes; oil's global price-setting mechanism; Trump administration 'energy independence' rhetoric vs. pump prices
framings.downplays: The global solidarity dimension, humanitarian context, non-oil commodities also disrupted
sample_headlines: Why no nation is truly 'energy independent' while the Strait of Hormuz remains closed (Fortune, May 2026)
Despite the United States being the largest oil producer in the world, it is still exposed to the same price shocks (Brookings, June 2026)

carriers.name: Fortune
carriers.excerpt: "leading President Donald Trump and others to tout the nation's 'energy independence'"
carriers.role_evidence: Fortune's piece was among the first major outlets to directly interrogate the gap between Trump's energy independence claims and the reality of gasoline price spikes, naming it as a political-rhetorical contradiction.

carriers.name: Brookings Institution
carriers.excerpt: "it is still exposed to the same price shocks as elsewhere because oil is a globally traded and largely fungible commodity"
carriers.role_evidence: Brookings provided academic grounding for the 'independence is illusory' argument while also noting that U.S. shale's slow supply response undermines the expansion argument.

carriers.name: Institute for Energy Research (IER)
carriers.excerpt: "the United States had 413 million barrels of strategic oil reserves, substantially less than the 714 million barrels of capacity"
carriers.role_evidence: IER, a conservative energy think tank, used the crisis to argue the opposite sub-framing: U.S. SPR depletion (blamed on Biden's 2022 releases) left America less protected than it should have been, calling for greater domestic energy posture.

carriers.name: EIA (Tristan Abbey, Administrator)
carriers.excerpt: "Our modeling indicates that fuel prices will continue to rise until these variables resolve"
carriers.role_evidence: EIA's official press release implicitly acknowledged the domestic price impact despite high U.S. production, providing data that critics of energy independence claims repeatedly cited.

carriers.name: Gulf International Forum
carriers.excerpt: "the United States has expanded exports from its shale sector, sending additional cargo to Asian markets while raising prices"
carriers.role_evidence: GIF noted the contradictory U.S. position: benefiting from shale export revenue gains while simultaneously suffering domestic price pain, complicating the independence narrative.

framings.name: War Accountability / Pre-War Decision-Making
framings.question: Were the U.S. and Israeli military decisions that triggered the closure foreseeable, and who bears responsibility for the resulting economic catastrophe?
framings.key_claim: The U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026, which Joint Chiefs of Staff had warned would prompt Hormuz closure, were a foreseeable cause of the supply disruption, making political decision-makers accountable for the economic consequences.
framings.description: This framing asks whether the civilian and military leaders who authorized the strikes on Iran acted recklessly given explicit warnings that Hormuz would be closed. It also encompasses Iran's legal accountability for attacking civilian shipping and the broader question of whether 'regime change' objectives justified the economic damage.
framings.emphasizes: Joint Chiefs warnings before February strikes, Trump administration's role in ordering the war, Iran's deliberate closure as a counter-measure, legality of Hormuz closure under international law, IRGC transit fees
framings.downplays: Iran's nuclear program threat, pre-existing tensions, the EIA's supply data itself

carriers.role_evidence: Wikipedia's continuously updated article aggregated the pre-war warning evidence most prominently and accessibly, making it the de facto reference point for the accountability framing.

carriers.name: Brookings Institution ('Blowback' series)

carriers.role_evidence: Brookings' 'Blowback' series explicitly framed the Hormuz disruption as a consequence of the decision to go to war, analyzing it as a failure of strategic foresight.

carriers.name: Congressional Research Service (CRS)
carriers.excerpt: "Congressional concern has risen in the wake of the February-March 2026 conflict"
carriers.role_evidence: CRS raised Congressional oversight questions about the military decision, implicitly institutionalizing the accountability framing within legislative branch deliberations.

carriers.name: House of Commons Library
carriers.excerpt: "They said they aimed to induce regime change in the country"
carriers.role_evidence: UK Parliament's research brief framed the crisis explicitly as a consequence of U.S.-Israeli regime-change objectives, giving the accountability framing parliamentary standing in an allied democracy.

carriers.name: World Economic Forum
carriers.excerpt: "The US-Israeli war with Iran has generated a media economy of its own"
carriers.role_evidence: WEF's 'global price tag' framing implicitly holds war-initiators accountable for economic consequences, though it stops short of direct attribution.

framings.name: Global South / Asymmetric Humanitarian Cost
framings.question: Who bears the disproportionate human cost—food insecurity, fuel shortages, inflation—of a disruption primarily caused by and serving the interests of major powers?
framings.key_claim: The Hormuz supply disruption inflicts its worst costs—food insecurity, fertilizer shortages, fuel poverty, and inflation—on import-dependent developing nations and Gulf civilian populations who had no role in the conflict that caused it.
framings.description: This framing centers the developing world, Gulf civilian populations, and vulnerable communities as the victims of a geopolitical conflict between major powers. It highlights fertilizer supply disruptions, food import dependence in Gulf states, inflation in South and Southeast Asia, and the asymmetry between U.S. economic insulation and global developing-nation exposure.
framings.emphasizes: 30%+ of global urea trade through Hormuz, food import emergency in Gulf states (80%+ caloric import dependence), Philippines/Vietnam/Pakistan fuel crises, $3.36B/month added to ASEAN's import bill, desalination plant attacks in Kuwait and Qatar
framings.downplays: OECD consumer pain, geopolitical power competition, military dimensions

carriers.name: UNCTAD

carriers.role_evidence: UNCTAD's report was the first major multilateral document centering developing-world trade and food-security impacts rather than OECD energy market effects.

carriers.name: IEA — Middle East and Global Energy Markets page
carriers.excerpt: "Fertiliser supply is particularly exposed. More than 30% of global trade of urea moves through the Strait"
carriers.role_evidence: IEA's thematic page explicitly documented fertilizer and food-security exposure, extending the disruption narrative beyond oil to humanitarian downstream effects.

carriers.name: World Bank
carriers.excerpt: "first through higher energy prices, then higher food prices, and finally, higher inflation"
carriers.role_evidence: World Bank's Commodity Markets Outlook adopted the asymmetric humanitarian framing, quantifying that developing economies face 5.1% inflation vs. pre-war forecasts.

carriers.name: Wikipedia — Economic impact of the 2026 Iran war
carriers.excerpt: "70% of the region's food imports were disrupted, forcing retailers like Lulu Retail to airlift staples"
carriers.role_evidence: Wikipedia's economic impact article aggregated the most granular humanitarian data (desalination plant attacks, grocery emergencies, Vietnam fuel queues) for a mass readership.

carriers.name: World Economic Forum
carriers.excerpt: "Asia's dependence on imported fossil fuels is turning geopolitical tensions into an economic strain"
carriers.role_evidence: WEF's Asia energy article amplified the asymmetric-burden framing to a global elite audience, quantifying ASEAN's $3.36B/month added import bill.

carriers.name: Discovery Alert (energy market analysis)
carriers.excerpt: "food security consequences of a prolonged Hormuz closure may outlast the energy market recovery by 6 to 18 months"
carriers.role_evidence: Specialist analysis platform introduced the agricultural-cycle delay argument—that food insecurity would persist 6–18 months after Hormuz reopens—extending the humanitarian framing beyond immediate crisis duration.

framings.name: International Law and Freedom of Navigation
framings.question: Is Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. counter-blockade lawful under international maritime law, and what precedent does this set?
framings.key_claim: Both Iran's declared closure of the Strait and the U.S. counter-blockade raise serious questions of legality under international maritime law, while Iran's potential transit-fee system would set a dangerous precedent for monetizing global chokepoints.
framings.description: This framing centers the legal and normative dimensions: the status of the Strait as an international waterway under UNCLOS, whether Iran's closure constitutes a violation, the legality of the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, the UN Security Council veto by China and Russia, and the IRGC's reported transit-fee scheme as extortion.
framings.emphasizes: UNCLOS freedom of transit passage, Iran's 'closed' declaration, U.S. counter-blockade legality, China/Russia UNSC veto, IRGC toll reports, Operation Aspides escort mission legal framework
framings.downplays: Economic price impacts, humanitarian suffering, energy transition implications

carriers.name: Wikipedia — 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis
carriers.excerpt: "China and Russia vetoed a draft resolution on the Strait of Hormuz"
carriers.role_evidence: Wikipedia's article is the primary mass-audience reference documenting the legal and UN dimensions—IRGC toll reports, UNSC veto, UNCLOS questions—aggregating sources from multiple legal and diplomatic outlets.

carriers.name: Brookings Institution
carriers.excerpt: "Allowing Iran to charge a toll in the Strait of Hormuz is deeply problematic"
carriers.role_evidence: Brookings flagged the IRGC transit-fee scheme as a normative threat to international maritime law, warning other countries might emulate it at chokepoints like Malacca.

carriers.name: Iranian Foreign Ministry (Esmaeil Baghaei)
carriers.excerpt: "sanctions against Oman would be illegal and contrary to the UN Charter and international law"

carriers.name: Congressional Research Service (CRS)

carriers.name: European Union (Kaja Kallas / Operation Aspides)

gap_analysis: Missing are framings centered on: (1) financial/investor perspectives—how markets, pension funds, and energy sector shareholders are positioned or harmed; (2) the role of non-state actors, private energy companies, and trading firms in either exacerbating or stabilizing the disruption; (3) technical/engineering solutions and infrastructure alternatives (pipelines, storage, LNG capacity) that bypass the strait; (4) domestic political economy within Middle Eastern producers themselves—internal pressure, regime stability, and competing interests among OPEC members. Also absent: perspectives from energy-poor nations or communities dependent on affordable oil for transport/heating, and any framing that questions the EIA's methodology or data reliability itself.
